sections.text: The COP31 UN climate summit has opened in Turkey. Berkeley Earth is 95% confident 2026 will be the hottest year on record, whilst the WMO forecasts it among the four warmest. sections.text: Top House Democrat Hakeem Jeffries announced he is a hard yes on impeaching Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth. Hegseth and the Pentagon rejected the accusations, calling them sham articles.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Massie alleges Hegseth violated the War Powers Resolution of 1973. While BBC News notes Jeffries is expected to become Speaker, The Guardian describes him as poised to become majority leader. sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Massie plans to introduce the resolution as early as Monday, and House Democrats plan to discuss it on Tuesday morning. Although Democrats hold a House majority, removing Hegseth requires a two-thirds Senate vote, which would require Republican support.

gist: The FDA requires GLP-1 drug makers to add warnings about a rare eye condition.
The condition, NAION, blocks blood flow to optic nerves and can cause permanent blindness.
Drugmakers note data has not established a cause-and-effect relationship between GLP-1s and NAION.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The US Food and Drug Administration ordered manufacturers of GLP-1 weight-loss and diabetes drugs, including Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, Zepbound and Soliqua, to add warning labels about nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy. NAION is a rare condition caused by reduced blood flow to the optic nerve, which can lead to sudden and permanent vision loss in one eye.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: An FDA review of clinical trials and studies indicated an increased risk of NAION among GLP-1 users. However, Novo Nordisk and the American Academy of Ophthalmology noted that a direct cause-and-effect link has not been established. Patients taking these drugs often already have separate NAION risk factors, such as diabetes and high blood pressure.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The American Academy of Ophthalmology advises patients not to stop taking GLP-1 medications without speaking to their doctor, and to consult an ophthalmologist immediately if sudden vision loss occurs.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Solange Alexandre, one of France's last World War Two resistance heroes, has died aged 104 at a nursing home in Le Mans. Starting as a courier in 1941, she later founded the Pas-de-Boeuf network and commanded about 30 men in sabotage and anti-German operations. She took part in the liberation of Tours and ended the war as a sub-lieutenant.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: She was a rare female commander of a resistance unit who served her country with distinction. President Emmanuel Macron paid tribute, stating that France will never forget her contribution.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: French police raided three properties linked to Mohamed Al Fayed, including the Ritz Paris hotel, Villa Windsor in Paris, and a villa in Saint-Tropez. Suspects were taken into police custody for questioning before being released. British Metropolitan Police officers attended the mid-October operations. Several alleged victims were also interviewed. Article 2 calls the Saint-Tropez property Castel Sainte-Thérèse, while French prosecutor statements refer to Villa Sainte-Thérèse.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The searches are part of a preliminary French investigation into allegations of human trafficking by an organised group, aggravated pimping, and rape. Campaign groups praised the French authorities' approach and urged British police to conduct similar searches of Fayed properties.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: French authorities are analysing digital material seized during the searches, and investigations continue under the Paris Public Prosecutor's Office. Survivor groups want the National Crime Agency to take over the investigation in Britain.

Big Walk used AI to fix a bug. Now the indie gaming world is having a reckoning.

gist: Independent Games Festival judges released a statement declining to vote for games using generative AI.
House House disclosed minimal AI use to fix a bug in Big Walk, sparking controversy.
Observers and jurors are divided on whether zero tolerance for minimal AI use is productive.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Nineteen IGF jurors published a statement refusing to vote for games using generative AI in any capacity. Following this, Big Walk developer House House disclosed that it sparingly used LLMs to help fix a difficult Unity engine bug near the end of development, representing well under 0.1 percent of the game's code.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The disclosure ignited a debate within the indie gaming community over transparency and zero tolerance policies. Some jurors argue that any AI use undermines human creativity and labor, while others feel transparency should be weighed against the scale of usage.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Jurors are urging the IGF to adopt a strong anti-clear policy for future years, while developers grapple with how disclosures will affect award consideration and community reception.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Andrew Johnson, an LNER train driver, testified at Cambridge Crown Court regarding a stabbing incident. While travelling at high speed, he received an alarm indicating a door was being tampered with. Upon hearing passengers screaming about a knifeman, he decided to divert the train to Huntingdon station. He requested police assistance and performed an unscheduled stop to allow passengers to escape.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The court is examining the actions of the driver during a violent event. Anthony Williams faces ten counts of attempted murder related to the train incident, alongside other charges in Peterborough and London. The central issue for the jury is determining whether the defendant possessed the intent to kill during these attacks.

gist: The UK and Argentina are debating offshore oil drilling at an international tribunal.
Argentina seeks to suspend the Sea Lion project, citing environmental risks and sovereignty claims.
The UK argues the project is vital for the Falkland Islands' economic development.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The UK and Argentina presented arguments to the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea in Hamburg. Argentina requested a suspension of the Sea Lion oil project, claiming it poses environmental risks and violates a 1976 UN resolution. The UK argued that the project is essential for the islands' economy and that the tribunal is not the appropriate venue for resolving sovereignty disputes.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The dispute highlights the ongoing tension over the sovereignty of the Falkland Islands. Argentina claims the resources belong to its people, while the UK asserts the islanders' right to self-determination and resource exploitation. The outcome could impact the future of the Sea Lion project, which is expected to begin drilling in March.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The tribunal hearing continues, with a decision pending on whether to issue provisional measures to suspend the drilling project.

gist: Startup PSI used AI to solve a long-standing quantum computing problem.
The company aims to commercialise theoretical physics breakthroughs using AI-driven research systems.
Researchers are currently establishing best practices for AI-generated scientific discoveries.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: David Turturean of the startup PSI used an AI model to solve the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, an 18-year-old quantum computing problem. The solution was autoformalized in the coding language Lean and verified by researchers. This result indicates that certain avenues for quantum computing speed are not viable.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The achievement highlights the growing capability of AI to solve complex scientific problems. PSI intends to build a business by using AI to generate theoretical physics breakthroughs that can be converted into new technologies. While AI excels in abstract fields like mathematics, applying these methods to physical sciences remains a challenge as models must be validated against real-world experiments.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The scientific community is working to define standards for AI-driven research. Experts are meeting at MIT to discuss best practices, focusing on transparency and expert verification as the pace of scientific discovery accelerates.

stories.standfirst: As espionage targets go, Jensen Huang is perhaps one of the least surprising on Earth. The Nvidia CEO runs one of the world's most valuable companies, controls the in-demand technology fueling the AI boom, and is cozy with presidents, CEOs, and all manner of important people.

timeline.text: The US is winning the AI race. Jensen Huang could have blown it

gist: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang faces scrutiny over an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
Experts warn the scandal could disrupt Nvidia's operations and threaten US AI leadership.
The situation may lead to stricter US legislation regarding AI chip exports to China.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang disclosed an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese intelligence operative. While no evidence suggests Huang shared trade secrets, the revelation has caused Nvidia's stock to decline and prompted concerns regarding potential security risks. Reports indicate companies linked to the individual facilitated significant chip sales to China.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Nvidia is a critical gatekeeper for advanced AI hardware. Experts suggest the scandal could distract company leadership, potentially slowing product rollouts and impacting major AI firms like OpenAI and Anthropic. Furthermore, there are concerns that Beijing could leverage access to Huang to gain insights into US industrial strategy and policy, or that the incident might disrupt the supply of scarce chips.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Ongoing investigations are expected to consume significant company resources. Analysts suggest the scandal will likely increase the probability of Congress passing more stringent legislation to control AI chip exports.

quotes.text: With those chips, the US lead could vanish in a matter of weeks or months.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: SpaceX introduced the Starlink Mini 2, a new satellite internet terminal. The device combines a dish, Wi-Fi router, and a battery into a single unit. It is thinner than the previous version at 23.1mm, though slightly heavier at 3.5 pounds. The terminal offers up to 4.5 hours of battery life, which can be extended through hot-swappable batteries or a USB-C power source.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The inclusion of a swappable battery enhances the portability of the satellite internet system. Maintaining an IP67 rating ensures the device remains suitable for outdoor use despite the new internal components.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The Starlink Mini 2 is currently available via invitation for select US customers. SpaceX intends to make the device available to more customers and countries in the future.

gist: Parents and advocacy groups are suing to block Washington state's new transgender sports ban.
The lawsuit claims the initiative violates privacy rights and discriminates against female student athletes.
The policy requires medical documentation of sex for girls wishing to join sports teams.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Voters in Washington state passed Initiative 638, which bans transgender girls from women’s sports teams. The measure requires girls to provide medical documentation regarding their sex, such as genetic tests or examinations of reproductive anatomy, to participate. A lawsuit has been filed by parents, TransFamilies, and the Washington Education Association to block the policy.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Plaintiffs argue the ban violates the state constitution by infringing on student privacy and discriminating against girls. Critics express concern that the enforcement mechanism could lead to invasive genital examinations, potentially discouraging all girls from participating in sports. Proponents maintain the ban is necessary to protect fairness in girls’ athletics.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The legal challenge is currently before the state court. The ban is scheduled to take effect on 3 December.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A report by the parliamentary and health service ombudsman revealed that disabled people in England wait up to two years for wheelchairs. Complaints regarding NHS wheelchair provision rose significantly. Issues include delays in receiving equipment or parts, and poor repairs. The investigation identified a regulatory gap where services like assessment and fitting are not supervised by health professionals, leaving them outside the remit of the Care Quality Commission.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Delays have profound consequences for users, including physical pain and emotional distress. Many are unable to attend school, access therapy, or maintain independence. The report notes that integrated care boards often lack reliable information on local needs and struggle with an uncompetitive market dominated by a few private firms.

sections.text: Former Guardian data journalist Mona Chalabi published her first book, Ten Lives, which mixes journalism, data visualisation and memoir. sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The book argues that collective ignorance and silence around personal income sustain an unfair system. It shows how systemic problems like lack of affordable care can easily overturn lives, driven by a fear of financial futures under advanced capitalism.

timeline.text: AI has made it ‘close to impossible’ to assess university coursework, regulator says

gist: AI makes assessing university coursework close to impossible according to a regulator investigation.
The Office for Students warns that degree credibility is under threat from AI use.
Universities are urged to return to traditional exams and in-person presentations.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: An investigation by the Office for Students and Advance HE found that artificial intelligence use in essays, dissertations and open book exams is widespread. Lecturers stated that coursework is now overwhelmingly written with the help of artificial intelligence, threatening academic integrity and making student assessment close to impossible.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The regulator warned that failing to design valid measures of students knowledge and skills could breach registration conditions and lead to sanctions. The situation presents a generational risk to the system, threatening to undermine students learning and institutional assessment abilities.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The Office for Students will continue working with universities and colleges to help them manage risks while reaping benefits. Institutions are encouraged to use more artificial intelligence free assessments, such as in-person written exams, oral examinations, and process-based tasks.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Hundreds of schools across Scotland, Northern Ireland, the Republic of Ireland and Italy received hoax bomb threat emails on Wednesday. Police assessed the threats as non-credible, noting they originated from generic distribution lists outside the UK. While most schools operated as normal, some local authorities evacuated pupils as a precaution.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The threats caused concern to pupils, parents and staff, coming less than a month after a similar wave of hoaxes. Authorities reassured the public that there was no credible risk, preventing widespread disruption.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Specialist cyber-crime officers and law enforcement bodies in the UK and overseas are working to identify those responsible. Schools have been advised to remain open and stay vigilant.

sections.text: The UK marked Armistice Day with a two-minute silence at 11:00. National services occurred at the Cenotaph in London and other locations including Edinburgh, Leeds and Conwy. sections.text: Consultant doctors in England have paused a two-day strike that was scheduled for 25 and 26 November. The British Medical Association, representing the doctors, decided to suspend the action to engage in formal negotiations with the government regarding pay and working conditions.

sections.text: The strike would have limited hospital services to emergency care only, likely causing delays for routine and elective procedures. gist: Millions in Spain joined the first general strike in 14 years over housing costs.
Transport and public services faced severe disruption across the country on Wednesday.
The strike occurred ahead of Spain’s general election on 29 November.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Millions of people across Spain joined a 24-hour general strike on Wednesday, disrupting transport, schools, ports and public services. Protesters set up roadblocks, dragged recycling bins into streets and vandalised short-term rental lockboxes. By midday, 27 people had been arrested during minor incidents.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The strike, organised by major unions and tenants' groups, targeted soaring housing costs and high living expenses. Rents have climbed 80% over a decade, while property prices rose 63%. Frustration intensified following recent evictions and the expansion of tourist rentals.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Spain holds a general election on 29 November. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called the snap vote after parliament rejected housing reform legislation. Polls indicate a possible rightwing coalition between the People's party and Vox.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Google DeepMind has unveiled AlphaGenome 2, an AI model designed to predict how genetic variants affect individual cell types and states. Trained on over 100 million cell profiles, the model provides a more detailed view of gene expression than its predecessor.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Understanding how specific genetic changes impact particular cells is crucial for medical research. By identifying these effects, scientists can better target proteins and cell types when developing new treatments for diseases.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: DeepMind is making the model available for non-commercial research via an API. Future development will focus on incorporating data from multiple species and potentially creating digital simulations of biological systems known as virtual cells.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The US midterm elections resulted in a defeat for Donald Trump’s Republicans and a Democratic-controlled Congress. While this outcome brought relief to some European capitals, experts warn that the US president may now use his foreign policy powers to act more aggressively on the world stage. European leaders remain concerned about potential trade tariffs and the impact on Ukraine.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The results have sparked debate over whether the US outcome signals a turning point for European politics. While some view it as a sign of democratic resilience, others note that populist parties in Europe remain strong. European mainstream parties face pressure to address issues like housing and inflation to avoid losing further ground to anti-system movements.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Europe faces critical upcoming tests, including a general election in Spain where a coalition between the Popular Party and the far-right Vox is possible. Meanwhile, European progressive parties are being urged to channel youth-led protest energy into meaningful political change to counter the appeal of nationalist populism.

gist: A new obesity diagnostic approach could reduce misdiagnosis rates globally.
The method combines BMI with waist measurements and organ function tests.
Experts suggest this approach improves individual healthcare and resource allocation.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Medical experts have proposed a new diagnostic approach for obesity to replace the current reliance on BMI. By incorporating waist measurements, weight-to-height ratios, and organ function tests, the method aims to distinguish between healthy individuals and those with harmful excess body fat. Researchers tested this approach using health records from over 800,000 people across four countries.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: BMI is considered a blunt instrument that frequently misclassifies millions of people. The new system identifies clinical obesity, where fat impairs organ function, versus pre-clinical obesity. This allows for more precise medical interventions, ranging from lifestyle advice to surgery, ensuring resources are used more effectively and safely.

fivew: Francisco Rubino and colleagues conducted the research.

gist: Argentina challenged UK oil drilling near the Falkland Islands at an international tribunal.
Argentina argues the UK acts like a colonial power regarding disputed maritime resources.
The UK maintains the tribunal lacks jurisdiction over sovereignty and disputes the urgency.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Argentina appeared before the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea in Hamburg. Legal representatives argued that the UK should not unilaterally authorise oil drilling in the North Basin of the Falkland Islands. Argentina requested a suspension of the Sea Lion project, citing a long-standing sovereignty dispute. The UK government countered that the tribunal lacks jurisdiction over sovereignty matters and argued that the project should proceed.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The dispute highlights ongoing tensions over the Falkland Islands, which Argentina claims as the Malvinas. Argentina contends that unilateral resource exploitation undermines its rights and represents colonial behaviour. Conversely, the UK maintains that the project is vital for the islands' economy and that the tribunal is not the appropriate venue for resolving the underlying sovereignty disagreement.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The UK is scheduled to provide further submissions to the tribunal. The panel of 20 judges will consider whether to order a suspension of drilling, which is currently planned to commence in March next year.

fivew: Legal teams representing Argentina and the UK.
Argentina is seeking to suspend UK-authorised oil drilling in disputed waters.
The hearing took place in Hamburg during the week of the report.
The case is being heard at the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Democrat Scott Colom defeated incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith in the Mississippi US Senate race. Colom won 49.2% of the vote compared to Hyde-Smith's 48.7%. Hyde-Smith conceded in a social media video, respecting the voters' decision and wishing Colom well.

sections.heading: Why it matters

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A large bronze limb discovered in a rural bog long ago was kept in a duke's storage area. Experts now think it belonged to a statue of Emperor Antoninus Pius situated near Hawick. sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The items demonstrate that Roman influence north of Hadrian's Wall was much greater than previously thought. The finds reveal details about imperial presence, trade, and the interaction between Roman forces and local iron-age communities.

timeline.text: Facial recognition errors put ethnic minorities at risk of wrongful arrest, police watchdog warns

gist: A watchdog warns facial recognition risks wrongful arrests, particularly among ethnic minorities.
Investigators sometimes treat technical probability scores as definitive proof instead of intelligence.
A report highlights outdated laws, algorithmic bias, and retained custody images.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A police watchdog published a report revealing that officers sometimes treat retrospective facial recognition results as concrete evidence rather than intelligence requiring further verification. The technology suffers from algorithmic bias, which disproportionately affects ethnic minorities, and issues with poor image quality and unlawfully retained custody images.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Using flawed technical data without sufficient human checks creates a significant danger of innocent people facing wrongful arrests. Furthermore, the absence of a comprehensive legal framework and safeguards threatens public trust in police forces.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Inspectors state that police forces must establish better safeguards, stricter national standards, and clearer governance to manage data retention and bias risks effectively.

fivew: A watchdog report warned about facial recognition errors risking wrongful arrests.
To address algorithmic bias, poor verification practices, and a lack of statutory safeguards.

quotes.text: Police forces must be able to show that appropriate safeguards are in place, risks relating to bias and data retention are effectively managed, and decisions are still subject to human judgment.

sections.text: Max strength cold medicines can cost significantly more than basic supermarket remedies. Many branded products contain extra ingredients like phenylephrine, but experts note oral tablets are largely ineffective.

gist: Levels of toxic PFOS and PFOA in English rivers dropped by nearly a third.
Stricter restrictions and bans on these forever chemicals drove the significant decline.
Thousands of other PFAS remain in use and require better monitoring and regulation.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: New Environment Agency figures show concentrations of PFOS and PFOA in English rivers fell by 30% and 29% respectively over the last decade following restrictions and bans.

sections.heading: Why it matters

sections.text: A 17-year-old named William went missing on a camping trip in bushland east of Melbourne, Victoria, and was found alive six days later. sections.text: Authorities were seriously concerned for the teenager's welfare because of the freezing overnight temperatures during his six-day disappearance. Police described the successful rescue as an emotional event that does not happen all the time.

articles.title: Oil slicks seen from space: the devastating impact of boat strikes on fragile Gulf ecosystems
articles.standfirst: Since the US war on Iran began in February, there have been hundreds of oil spills, posing a ‘generational’ threat to wildlife

timeline.text: Oil slicks seen from space: the devastating impact of boat strikes on fragile Gulf ecosystems

gist: War in the Gulf causes massive oil spills threatening fragile marine ecosystems.
Satellite imagery reveals extensive pollution from vessel strikes and naval blockades.
Experts warn of generational environmental damage similar to past conflicts.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Throughout the war between the US and Iran, oil tankers and naval vessels have been struck by missiles or sea mines in the strait of Hormuz, spilling crude oil into the sea. Greenpeace identified more than 500 instances of oil spills across the region since February, covering a cumulative total of approximately 20,000 square kilometres.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The pollution has contaminated coastlines and threatens coral reefs, mangrove forests and marine life. Because the Gulf is shallow and warm, it lacks deep water to buffer the heat and pollution. Past conflicts show oil can remain trapped in sediments for decades, creating a generational environmental problem.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Environmental organisations are continuing to analyse satellite imagery, although on-the-ground investigations remain extremely difficult. Some bordering countries have responded to spills by closing beaches, launching cleanups and monitoring desalination plants, but wider environmental damage will be hard to contain.

In the Gulf, the strait of Hormuz and the Arabian Sea.
Military conflict in a busy shipping route has turned the waterway into a battlefield.

quotes.text: Since the Gulf is shallow, and summer is the least windy period of the year, atmospheric heat is rapidly translated into ocean heat.

sections.text: Intensified Russian attacks on Ukraine's energy grid have damaged power stations and substations, forcing rolling blackouts across the country. sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The UK economy expanded by 0.7% in the third quarter, making it the second-fastest growing G7 economy this year. This expansion defied gloomy Treasury and City analyst forecasts of near-zero growth.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Growth was powered by IT, professional services, and household consumption. AI-related spending contributed an estimated 0.3% to 0.4% to GDP growth, supported by datacentre investment. However, market fears surrounding an AI stock bubble threaten future tech investment.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: A difficult winter lies ahead as energy bills increase in January, inflation approaches 5%, and real wage growth cools. The Bank of England is expected to raise interest rates to 4.5%, adding further pressure to living costs.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Two Iranian asylum seekers living in west London, Mostafa Sepahvand and Farhad Javadi Manesh, were convicted at Woolwich Crown Court of assisting a foreign intelligence service. gist: The City of Birmingham Symphony Orchestra performed Britten's War Requiem at Coventry Cathedral.
The concert marked Armistice Day and 50 years since Britten's own death.
Kazuki Yamada conducted soloists Andrew Staples, Christian Gerhaher, Olga Peretyatko and several choruses.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The City of Birmingham Symphony Orchestra performed Britten's War Requiem at Coventry Cathedral, conducted by Kazuki Yamada. The performance featured soloists Andrew Staples, Christian Gerhaher and Olga Peretyatko, alongside the CBSO Chorus, CBSO Youth Chorus and Trinity Boys Choir.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The concert took place where the work premiered in 1962, marking Armistice Day and 50 years since Britten's own death. Some boy choristers from the original premiere attended.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The performance is available on BBC Sounds until 10 December.

timeline.text: Teenage girl admits murder in row over boy

gist: Kayla Smith admitted murdering 16-year-old Chloe Watson Dransfield in a fight over a boy.
Blake Dowling and Archie Rycroft remain on trial for murder and manslaughter.
Mr Justice Cavanagh KC will sentence Smith to life imprisonment after the trial finishes.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Kayla Smith, 18, admitted murdering 16-year-old Chloe Watson Dransfield at Leeds Crown Court. Smith fatally stabbed Chloe five times during a pre-planned fight over Blake Dowling in Leeds on 28 March. Dowling took Chloe to the scene, whilst Archie Rycroft accompanied Smith. Both men remain on trial for murder and manslaughter.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The trial of Dowling and Rycroft will continue. Mr Justice Cavanagh KC stated he will sentence Smith after their trial finishes, noting that murder carries a mandatory life sentence with a minimum term to be determined.

Kayla Smith fatally stabbed 16-year-old Chloe Watson Dransfield during a pre-planned fight.
The attack happened in the early hours of 28 March.
The stabbing occurred at a house in Kennerleigh Avenue, Leeds.
The stabbing followed an argument over a shared boyfriend, Blake Dowling.

articles.standfirst: Shares up 7% after announcement as Jaime Gilinski Bacal seeks exit three years after helping to rescue bank

timeline.text: Metro Bank up for sale, with billionaire investor in line for £420m windfall

gist: Metro Bank has publicly announced that it is putting itself up for sale.
Billionaire Jaime Gilinski Bacal could gain a £420m windfall from the sale.
The bank stated it can remain independent if no suitable buyer is found.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Metro Bank has publicly announced it is open to takeover bids, three years after its near-collapse. The decision increased its share price by 7% on Thursday morning, valuing the bank at around £1.3bn.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: A sale could yield a windfall of over £420m for Colombian billionaire investor Jaime Gilinski Bacal, who bought a 53% stake during a £925m rescue deal in 2023. Chief executive Daniel Frumkin has since cut over 1,000 jobs and closed Sunday branches to improve profitability.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Metro Bank's board believes assessing buyer interest will maximise shareholder value, but noted that a sale is only one option and it could remain independent.

gist: Tim Westwood pleaded not guilty to two additional sexual offences in court.
He now faces 17 total charges involving nine women spanning decades.
A trial is scheduled for January at Southwark Crown Court.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: During a court appearance, Tim Westwood entered not guilty pleas for two further charges. One involves an allegation from 1991 in west London, while the second relates to an incident in south London in 2004. These additions bring his total number of denied charges to 17 concerning nine complainants.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The case involves numerous historical allegations against a prominent former broadcaster, with charges covering a long timeframe from the 1980s through to the 2010s.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The defendant remains on conditional bail and is scheduled to face a seven-week trial beginning on 27 January at Southwark Crown Court.

gist: Crystal Palace sacked their manager after a poor run of form.
The team has been winless in the league since October.
Injuries and player absences impacted the squad's performance.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Crystal Palace have sacked boss Sage after 16 games following a winless league run stretching back to 11 October. The decline began with a heavy defeat against rivals Brighton, and three successive losses followed despite hitting the bar and having a goal ruled out against Liverpool.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Sage managed only five wins in 16 matches across all competitions. His plans were hampered by injuries and the absence of forwards Jean-Philippe Mateta and Ismaila Sarr due to fitness and personal issues related to their desire to leave the club.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Crystal Palace's next Premier League match is scheduled away at Coventry on 21 November, following the international break.

timeline.text: Brilliant Noskova dismantles Gauff to reach WTA Finals last four

gist: Linda Noskova defeated Coco Gauff to reach the WTA Finals semi-finals.
Noskova secured victory in straight sets during her tournament debut.
Jessica Pegula eliminated Marta Kostyuk from the competition.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Linda Noskova beat Coco Gauff 6-3 6-3 to become the first player to reach the WTA Finals semi-finals. Noskova served well and hit powerful winners throughout the match. Meanwhile, Jessica Pegula defeated Marta Kostyuk 6-2 7-5 to earn her first win since September.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The victory marks a sixth top-10 win this season for Noskova, who won Wimbledon in July. Gauff struggled on serve, hitting eight aces and eight double faults. Pegula remains in contention for the last four alongside Gauff.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Noskova has secured her place in the semi-finals. Gauff and Pegula can still qualify for the last four.

fivew: Linda Noskova defeated Coco Gauff to reach the WTA Finals semi-finals.
The match took place during the WTA Finals.
The tournament is held in California.

sections.text: Chelsea lost 1-0 to Sunderland after Brian Brobbey won a penalty that Enzo le Fee converted. Referee decisions went against Chelsea, and manager Xabi Alonso criticised his players for failing to execute the gameplan.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Constant tinkering and a mounting injury list have hindered Alonso's attempts to establish a consistent style of play, though the team remains fifth in the table.

gist: Brighton climbed to second in the Premier League after beating Brentford 2-0.
The Seagulls sit five points behind league leaders Arsenal after ten matches.
Midfielder Pascal Gross downplayed any suggestions that his side are in a title race.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Brighton defeated Brentford 2-0 at the Amex Stadium on Sunday afternoon. The victory lifted the Seagulls into second place in the Premier League, moving them above Manchester City before the November international break.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Brighton have won seven of their opening ten matches, establishing themselves as the closest challengers to league leaders Arsenal with a five-point gap. Their strong underlying numbers and defensive record suggest they could maintain this early-season form.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Brighton head into the international break aiming to maintain their momentum for the remainder of the campaign, while awaiting the return of injured players like Kaoru Mitoma.

timeline.text: Bizarre & thrilling theatre as Carrick's Man Utd future still in limbo

gist: Manchester United drew four-all with Aston Villa after scoring a stoppage-time equaliser.
Manager Michael Carrick remains in his position despite United dropping into the relegation zone.
Fans protested against club owners and ticket prices amid poor league form.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Manchester United drew four-all against Aston Villa in an eight-goal thriller at Old Trafford. United fought back twice from two goals down, securing a point with a ninety-sixth-minute equaliser from Patrick Dorgu. The result left United in eighteenth place in the relegation zone during the international break.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: United are in their lowest league position for forty years after playing at least ten matches, having failed to win a league game since August. The poor form has intensified pressure on manager Michael Carrick and sparked unprecedented fan protests against ticket prices and club ownership.
